title: Set Matrix Zeroes
description: Brute force to optimized: tracking zero-rows/columns in separate sets versus repurposing the matrix's own first row and column as O(1) marker storage.

blocks.text: Given an m x n integer matrix matrix, if an element is 0, set its ENTIRE row and ENTIRE column to 0, doing this in place.

blocks.caption: Use the first row and first column themselves as markers, avoiding extra storage

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An m x n integer matrix matrix"],["Output","The same matrix, modified in place, with every row and column containing a 0 fully zeroed out"],["Goal","Achieve this using as little extra space as possible, ideally O(1)"],["Constraints","m == matrix.length; n == matrix[i].length; 1 <= m, n <= 200; -2^31 <= matrix[i][j] <= 2^31 - 1"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Need to remember WHICH rows and columns contain a 0, before zeroing anything","Some form of marker/tracking mechanism is needed, separate from the actual zeroing step"],["An O(1) space solution is explicitly desired (a common follow-up in this exact problem)","Reuse part of the existing matrix itself (its first row and first column) as the marker storage, instead of allocating separate sets"],["The first row and first column are themselves part of the matrix, and could also legitimately need zeroing","Save their own \"should this be zeroed\" status in two separate boolean flags BEFORE using them as markers for everything else"]]}

blocks.text: Given a matrix, if any cell is 0, zero out that cell's entire row and entire column, doing this transformation in place.

blocks.title: Analogy: Marking a Spreadsheet's Header Row and Column as a Reference
blocks.text: Like scanning a spreadsheet for any cell containing an error marker, and needing to blank out every row and column containing such a marker. Rather than keeping a separate scratch list of "which rows/columns need blanking", the spreadsheet's own header row and header column can be repurposed as that exact scratch space, since they'll be blanked out anyway if they themselves ever need it.

blocks.caption: Row 0 and column 0 double as marker storage, checked and applied in a later pass

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["A single 0 is found at position (1,1)","Row 1 and column 1 need zeroing","Every cell in row 1 and every cell in column 1 must become 0"],["Answer","[[1,0,1],[0,0,0],[1,0,1]]","Row 1 is entirely 0, and column 1 is entirely 0, while everything else stays unchanged"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Zeros are found at (0,0) and (0,3)","Rows 0 needs zeroing (twice, harmlessly); columns 0 and 3 need zeroing","Every cell in row 0, column 0, and column 3 must become 0"],["Answer","[[0,0,0,0],[0,4,5,0],[0,3,1,0]]","Row 0 is entirely 0, column 0 is entirely 0, and column 3 is entirely 0, while other cells stay unchanged"]]}

blocks.text: Before allocating separate storage to remember which rows and columns contain a zero, notice that the matrix's own first row and first column can serve exactly that purpose.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Zeroing must happen based on the ORIGINAL positions of zeros, not zeros introduced by the zeroing process itself, so some way of remembering "which rows/columns originally had a zero" is needed before any zeroing begins.

Observation 2: Rather than using separate sets or arrays for this bookkeeping, the matrix's own first row and first column can be repurposed as marker storage: matrix[i][0] can mark "row i needs zeroing", and matrix[0][j] can mark "column j needs zeroing".

Observation 3: Since the first row and first column are themselves being repurposed as markers, their OWN original "did this row/column originally have a zero" status must be saved separately (in two simple boolean flags) before this marking process begins, so they can be correctly zeroed (or not) at the very end.

Observation 4: After marking, a second pass reads the markers (matrix[i][0] and matrix[0][j]) to zero out the interior of the matrix, and a final step applies the two saved boolean flags to correctly finish off the first row and first column themselves.

Recognizing that part of the existing data structure can double as its own bookkeeping mechanism is what eliminates the need for separate O(m+n) marker storage.
This is a space-reduction technique: repurposing part of an existing data structure (here, the first row and column) as scratch storage, rather than allocating new memory for that bookkeeping.
Use separate sets to remember every row and column that contains at least one zero, then zero out matching cells in a second pass.

items: Scan the entire matrix once, recording every row index and column index that contains at least one zero.
Scan the matrix again, setting any cell to 0 if its row or column was recorded in the first pass.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The two sets (zeroRows, zeroCols) are built entirely before any zeroing happens, ensuring only ORIGINAL zero positions are ever recorded.
The second pass zeroes a cell if EITHER its row or its column was recorded, correctly covering both requirements.
This clean separation of "record" then "apply" avoids any interference between reading original values and writing new zeros.

blocks.text: Every zero is correctly identified and its entire row and column are correctly zeroed, so the result is always accurate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows * cols), with two full passes over the matrix.
Space: O(rows + cols) for the two sets tracking which rows and columns need zeroing.

Limitation: allocating separate sets to track zero-rows and zero-columns uses O(rows + cols) extra space, when the matrix's own first row and first column could instead be repurposed to store exactly this same information, achieving O(1) extra space.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force uses separate sets for tracking. Instead, first save whether the first row and first column ORIGINALLY contained a zero, in two simple boolean flags. Then, scanning only the interior of the matrix (rows and columns from index 1 onward), whenever a zero is found at (i, j), mark matrix[i][0] and matrix[0][j] as zero, repurposing the first row and column as the marker storage. A second pass over the interior then zeroes any cell whose row-marker or column-marker is set. Finally, use the two saved boolean flags to correctly zero the first row and/or first column themselves, if they originally needed it.

Save firstRowHasZero and firstColHasZero by checking the original first row and column. Scan the interior (rows 1+, columns 1+), marking matrix[i][0] and matrix[0][j] to 0 wherever a zero is found. Scan the interior again, zeroing any cell whose row-marker or column-marker is 0. Finally, zero the entire first row if firstRowHasZero was true, and the entire first column if firstColHasZero was true.
Repurpose the first row and column as marker storage, saving their own original zero-status in two flags first.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Action","Matrix / flags state"],"rows":[["1","Save flags: firstRowHasZero = false (row 0 is [1,1,1]); firstColHasZero = false (column 0 is [1,1,1])","flags: false, false"],["2","Scan interior: found a 0 at (1,1); mark matrix[1][0]=0 and matrix[0][1]=0","[[1,0,1],[0,0,1],[1,1,1]]"],["3","Apply markers to interior: matrix[1][1] already 0 (row/col marker match); matrix[1][2] checked against matrix[1][0]=0, becomes 0; matrix[2][1] checked against matrix[0][1]=0, becomes 0","[[1,0,1],[0,0,0],[1,0,1]]"],["4","firstRowHasZero and firstColHasZero are both false, so row 0 and column 0 are left as they are (already correctly updated by the marker process itself)","[[1,0,1],[0,0,0],[1,0,1]]"]]}

blocks.title: Final result
blocks.text: The final matrix [[1,0,1],[0,0,0],[1,0,1]] matches the expected answer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows * cols), across the marking pass, the applying pass, and the initial/final flag-based row/column checks.
Space: O(1) extra, using only two boolean flags beyond the matrix itself.

Since the interior of the matrix (rows/columns 1 and beyond) is scanned first to place markers into the first row and column, and only afterward is that marker information used to zero the interior, no legitimate original data is lost before it's needed. The first row and column's own original zero-status, saved in two flags before any marking begins, ensures they can still be correctly zeroed (or correctly left alone) at the very end, even though they were simultaneously being used as scratch space throughout the process.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A zero is found in the interior at (i, j)","matrix[i][0] and matrix[0][j] are both marked to 0, flagging that row i and column j need zeroing"],["Applying markers to the interior","Any interior cell whose row marker or column marker is 0 gets zeroed"],["Finishing the first row/column","Zeroed entirely only if their ORIGINAL (saved) status indicated they contained a zero"]]}

items: The two boolean flags are computed FIRST, before any marker-writing begins, capturing the true original state of the first row and column.
The marking and applying passes both explicitly start from index 1, deliberately excluding the first row and column, which are handled separately at the very end.
The final two conditional zeroing steps use the saved flags, not the (possibly already-modified) current state of the first row/column.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (separate row/column sets)","O(rows * cols)","O(rows + cols)","Uses extra sets to track which rows and columns need zeroing"],["Optimized (first row/column as markers, O(1) space)","O(rows * cols)","O(1) extra","Repurposes the matrix's own first row and column as marker storage"]]}

blocks.text: Repurposing part of an existing data structure as its own bookkeeping/marker storage, carefully preserving whatever original information from that part is still needed, is a powerful technique for reducing auxiliary space to O(1).

items: Forgetting to save the first row/column's ORIGINAL zero-status before using them as markers, causing incorrect results if they're later checked using their (by-then-modified) current values instead.
Marking and applying in the same single pass, which can cause a marker placed early to incorrectly zero a cell that hasn't been checked yet, corrupting the "original value" needed for a later check.
Forgetting to start the interior scans from index 1 (not 0), which would incorrectly treat the first row/column as ordinary interior cells.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["matrix has no zeros at all","The matrix is returned completely unchanged, since neither flag is ever set and no markers are ever placed"],["A zero exists specifically at (0, 0)","Both firstRowHasZero and firstColHasZero become true, correctly zeroing the entire first row AND column"],["matrix has only 1 row or 1 column","The interior loops (starting at index 1) simply do nothing, and the two flag-based final steps handle everything correctly"]]}

items: Explicitly walk through WHY the first row/column's original status must be saved before being repurposed as markers, since this exact subtlety is the most common point of confusion (and the detail interviewers most often probe) in this specific O(1)-space solution.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Modify a matrix in place based on some property of its cells, using O(1) extra space" points toward repurposing part of the matrix itself (often a border row/column) as scratch marker storage, carefully preserving whatever original data from that part is still needed.

items: Why does the marking pass need to run to completion BEFORE the applying pass begins? If they were merged into a single pass, a marker placed early (say, at row 2) could incorrectly cause a later cell in that same row to be zeroed before its original value has even been checked for being a zero itself.

How would this generalize to a "set to zero" rule based on some other condition, not just literal zeros? The same technique (mark using part of the structure, save that part's own original state first, apply, then finish that part) generalizes directly to any similar in-place marking problem.

What if the matrix were extremely sparse (very few zeros among a huge matrix)? A set-based approach (the brute force here) could actually use LESS memory in that specific case, since it only stores as many entries as there are actual zero rows/columns, rather than a fixed O(1) but still requiring a full O(rows*cols) time pass regardless.

A space-reduction technique reusing part of the existing matrix as auxiliary storage, conceptually related to in-place array manipulation techniques used elsewhere in this category (e.g., Rotate Image's in-place transpose-and-reverse), but here repurposing data rather than just rearranging it.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(rows * cols) time, O(rows + cols) space.
Optimized (first row/column as markers): O(rows * cols) time, O(1) extra space.

items: Pattern: Repurposing the matrix's own first row and column as O(1) marker storage, with their original state saved in two flags first
Core Idea: Mark needed rows/columns using the first row/column itself, apply those markers to the interior, then finish the first row/column using the pre-saved flags
Time: O(rows * cols)
Space: O(1) extra
Most Important Observation: Part of an existing data structure can often double as its own scratch storage, as long as whatever original information it holds is saved before being overwritten
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Save first row/col flags, mark using row 0/col 0, apply to interior, then finish row 0/col 0 using the saved flags
